title: Ethical Dilemmas and Patient Advocacy

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

The word dilemma gets used loosely for anything hard, but in ethics it means something specific: both options have real ethical weight behind them, and choosing one costs you the other. Compare that to three situations people confuse it with. If you just need more information, that is a puzzle, and more data solves it. If you already know the right move but something is blocking you, that is a different problem with a different fix. If the law already answers it, there was never a live choice. Only the genuine collision of two legitimate duties requires the kind of deliberation ethics offers.

### Question 2

Advocacy is often misread as one of two things it is not: talking the patient into the recommended plan, or taking the decision off their hands. Both replace the patient's voice with someone else's. The actual function is closer to interpretation and amplification. The healthcare system moves fast, uses its own vocabulary, and has a steep authority gradient, so a patient's concern can be raised and still not land. The advocate makes sure it lands, and makes sure the version that lands is the patient's version, not a cleaned-up one that happens to agree with the team.

### Question 3

Moral distress has a precise definition worth holding onto, because it is routinely mislabeled as burnout. Burnout is depletion; compassion fatigue is the cost of absorbing others' suffering; both are largely about the clinician's internal reserves. Moral distress is about agency. Something outside you stands between you and the action your professional judgment points toward. Notice that AACN's definition deliberately covers uncertainty too, so you can be genuinely unsure what is right and still be morally distressed by being unable to pursue the question. Because the source of the problem sits outside the individual, individual coping strategies alone will not resolve it.

### Question 4

Both feel like being stuck, which is why students blur them, but they are stuck in different places. In a dilemma the difficulty is upstream, at the judgment: you have not yet settled which obligation should win, because more than one has a real claim. In moral distress the judgment is already made or at least in progress, and the difficulty is downstream, at the doing. That difference tells you where to push. Talking a dilemma through with the right people can genuinely resolve it. Talking through moral distress may help you endure it, but nothing changes until the thing blocking you does.

### Question 5

The most common misconception is that an ethics committee decides the case. It generally does not, and the reason is practical rather than modest. The moment a consultation service can punish you or hand down a binding verdict, staff and families stop bringing it their hardest situations, and the service loses access to exactly the cases it exists for. So its authority is persuasive: it gets the clinicians, the family, the chaplain, and the social worker into one conversation, surfaces what each party actually values, and puts a reasoned option on the table. Allocation of scarce resources and staff discipline run through separate structures.

### Question 6

Intuition says repeated exposure should dull the response, the way it does with most unpleasant things. Moral distress runs the other way, and understanding why is the point of this item. Each unresolved episode leaves residue, a sense of having acted against your own standards that does not clear on its own. The next situation therefore does not start from zero; it lands on top of everything still unsettled, so the reaction climbs rather than flattens. That rising curve is the crescendo effect, and it explains a pattern that otherwise looks strange: the nurses who care most about doing right are often the ones who leave.

### Question 7

Sort the options by what each one actually changes. Resilience training changes the person absorbing the problem. Reassignment changes who is standing in front of the problem. An annual survey changes nothing until next year, by which point the patient's case is long closed. Only one option changes the thing that produced the distress, by creating a route through which a concern raised today gets acted on today. That is the general test worth carrying forward: since moral distress comes from a constraint, an intervention that leaves the constraint untouched can at best make the distress easier to tolerate.

### Question 8

Work through these by asking what would actually make the difficulty go away. For the new confusion in option A, a workup would; that is a clinical puzzle. For the dressing frequency in option C, a conversation with the prescriber would; that is a clarification. For the chart request in option D, the rule already supplies the answer and the remaining work is explaining it kindly; that is a legal and communication task. For the transfusion refusal in option B, nothing dissolves the difficulty, because two obligations you are genuinely bound by point in opposite directions and honoring one costs the other. That residue left after everything else has been cleared away is the mark of a real dilemma.

### Question 9

Three of these options are things a caring nurse might genuinely do, which is what makes the item worth thinking through. Reassurance is comfortable for everyone and moves nothing. Detailed documentation is professionally necessary and creates a record, but a record is not a message; nobody has to read it today. Coaching the patient to speak up sounds empowering until you notice that this patient already spoke up and was interpreted as anxious, so it returns the burden to the person with the least leverage in the room. Advocacy means the concern travels, with your assessment attached, and keeps traveling upward until someone acts.

### Question 10

Skipping straight to the options is the most common failure in real ethics discussions, and it is expensive. Cases regularly collapse at the fact-checking stage because the prognosis everyone was arguing about had been superseded, or because a daughter's objection turns out to rest on something she was told incorrectly two days ago, or because nobody has yet asked the patient. Naming the stakeholders and the specific values in tension does the second half of the work: it converts a vague sense that something is wrong into a statement of what exactly is competing with what, and options can only be compared once that statement exists.

### Question 11

The same belief, held with the same sincerity, produces either a protected professional act or a licensure problem depending on two variables that have nothing to do with the belief itself. The first is timing: an objection raised before you accept responsibility can be planned around, while one raised after leaves a gap in real time. The second is transfer: someone competent must be holding the patient's care when you step back. Note also what conscientious objection is aimed at. It is a refusal to participate in a specific intervention, not a refusal to care for a particular person, and refusing the person moves into discrimination rather than conscience.

### Question 12

Law, organizational policy, and ethics are three separate systems that usually converge, and the interesting work begins where they do not. Two opposite errors are tempting. The first treats the policy manual as if it settled the ethics, which the ANA Code rejects explicitly: compliance without discernment is not integrity. The second treats private moral conviction as a license to override the rule quietly, which fails for a practical reason as much as a professional one. A policy worked around in silence stays in force and harms the next patient, while a policy formally challenged through consultation, chain of command, or review can actually be rewritten.
